title: The Yankee and Cowboy War: Conspiracies from Dallas to Watergate
author: Carl Oglesby

chapters.title: Yankees and Cowboys: A Perspective on the Dallas–Watergate Decade
The Whole Bay of Pigs Thing

notes: PDF page numbers are 1-based. Main-text printed page equals PDF page minus 16.
OCR inspected against rendered PDF page 63; noisy OCR needs cautious treatment.
Yankee and Cowboy are Oglesby’s analytical faction labels, not formal membership organizations.
The author distinguishes his hypotheses from established facts in several passages; preserve attribution on disputed assassination, intelligence and cover-up claims.
PDF 61 OCR dates Ford pardon to 1971; avoid treating this as an independently verified event date.
The author’s account of Gehlen and the CIA contains chronology and institutional claims requiring external corroboration; retained as source claims only.

people.name: Carl Oglesby
people.description: Oglesby describes his interpretation of Dallas and Watergate as struggles between rival power elites and notes that faction labels are an analytical model.

people.name: John F. Kennedy
people.description: Oglesby describes a president whose coalition faced internal disputes over Cuba, Vietnam, taxation and civil rights; the proposed connection to his murder is the author’s theory.

people.name: Richard Nixon
people.description: Oglesby describes Nixon’s June 1972 taped references to Bay of Pigs as a clue connecting Watergate to earlier clandestine conflicts.

people.name: John Mitchell
people.description: Oglesby describes the attorney general implicated in Liddy’s reported explanation of the proposed Greenspun burglary.

people.name: Howard Hughes
people.description: Oglesby describes an emblem of entrepreneurial Cowboy wealth and an employer of Robert Maheu; his connection to Watergate is explored provisionally.

people.name: Robert Maheu
people.description: Oglesby describes a Hughes operative who acted between the CIA and John Roselli in a plot against Castro.

people.name: J. Edgar Hoover
people.description: Oglesby describes the director signing domestic counterintelligence instructions and providing the commission information about Oswald, ballistics and Ruby.

people.name: Allen W. Dulles
people.description: Oglesby describes a CIA leader and Warren commissioner; the author discusses his responses to possible Oswald intelligence connections.

people.name: Carroll Quigley
people.description: Oglesby describes the historian whose account of the Round Table supplies a foundation for Oglesby’s interpretation of elite power.

people.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
people.description: Oglesby describes the president whose Vietnam escalation and 1968 withdrawal from candidacy Oglesby frames through factional conflict.

people.name: Robert F. Kennedy
people.description: Oglesby describes Kennedy’s anti-organized-crime campaign, feud with Johnson and 1968 coalition, followed by assassination.

people.name: John Connally
people.description: Oglesby describes the governor wounded beside Kennedy, who later testified that he believed a separate bullet hit him.

people.name: E. Howard Hunt
people.description: Oglesby describes a participant in anti-Castro operations whose knowledge worried Nixon in the tapes.

people.name: H. R. Haldeman
people.description: Oglesby describes Nixon’s interlocutor in the June 23, 1972 conversations concerning CIA involvement and Bay of Pigs.

people.name: Richard Helms
people.description: Oglesby describes the director referenced in discussions with FBI acting director Gray and in a Mexico City memorandum.

people.name: L. Patrick Gray
people.description: Oglesby describes Gray’s reported conversation with Helms about whether Watergate touched a covert operation.

people.name: Fidel Castro
people.description: Oglesby describes the target of the invasion and assassination schemes discussed in the book.

people.name: John Roselli
people.description: Oglesby describes the figure Maheu contacted on behalf of the CIA for operations against Castro.

people.name: Meyer Lansky
people.description: Oglesby describes a central Syndicate figure in the author’s account of wartime cooperation and pre-revolutionary Cuban gambling.

people.name: Charles Lucky Luciano
people.description: Oglesby describes the imprisoned leader whose wartime cooperation and eventual release are described as foundations of Operation Underworld.

people.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
people.description: Oglesby describes the wartime president whom Oglesby holds politically responsible for cooperation with organized crime.

people.name: Fulgencio Batista
people.description: Oglesby describes Lansky’s Cuban partner in the author’s account of liquor sourcing, gambling and political influence.

people.name: Bebe Rebozo
people.description: Oglesby describes a Florida businessman whose friendship with Nixon and business links Oglesby examines, separating possible early contacts from established later relationships.

people.name: Richard Danner
people.description: Oglesby describes a former FBI man and Miami Beach city manager described as a connector among Nixon, Rebozo and Hughes.

people.name: George Smathers
people.description: Oglesby describes a Rebozo business partner and Nixon acquaintance who, in an anecdote quoted by Oglesby, pressed Kennedy to kill Castro.

people.name: Reinhard Gehlen
people.description: Oglesby describes the former Nazi intelligence officer whose postwar arrangement with American officials the author treats as a source of clandestine influence.

people.name: Andrei Vlassov
people.description: Oglesby describes an anti-Bolshevik commander whom Oglesby links to Gehlen’s wartime intelligence sources.

people.name: William Donovan
people.description: Oglesby describes an American intelligence leader named among Gehlen’s interlocutors.

people.name: Walter Bedell Smith
people.description: Oglesby describes the general whose command transport carried Gehlen to Washington in the author’s account.

people.name: Lee Harvey Oswald
people.description: Oglesby describes the accused gunman whose life and possible intelligence contacts Oglesby disputes; his role as a loyal CIA infiltrator is explicitly speculative.

people.name: Marina Oswald
people.description: Oglesby describes Oswald’s Russian wife accompanying him on his return to the United States.

people.name: Jack Ruby
people.description: Oglesby describes Oswald’s killer and a key witness whom Oglesby interprets as possibly attempting to reveal more than the commission elicited.

people.name: Earl Warren
people.description: Oglesby describes the chairman whose investigation and motives are critically assessed, with the nuclear-war-cover-up explanation expressly presented as a hypothesis.

people.name: Gerald Ford
people.description: Oglesby describes a commissioner participating in secret deliberations and Ruby’s hearing, later the president pardoning Nixon.

people.name: Arlen Specter
people.description: Oglesby describes the counsel associated with the single-bullet theory and Ruby’s examination.

people.name: J. Lee Rankin
people.description: Oglesby describes the lawyer managing the commission’s deliberation over allegations of Oswald intelligence ties.

people.name: Harold Weisberg
people.description: Oglesby describes a Warren critic whose litigation obtained records of ballistics analysis and secret commission sessions.

people.name: Peter Dale Scott
people.description: Oglesby describes the researcher whose interpretations of Oswald’s discharge and Ruby’s crime connections Oglesby cites.

people.name: George O’Toole
people.description: Oglesby describes the advocate using voice-stress analysis to argue Oswald’s denials were truthful; this disputed technique is not validated by the archive.

people.name: George de Mohrenschildt
people.description: Oglesby describes an associate who befriended the Oswalds, whose intelligence affiliation is asserted by Oglesby and remains source-attributed.

people.name: Clay Shaw
people.description: Oglesby describes the figure linked to Oswald and Ferrie through claims cited from Marchetti and witnesses; those affiliations remain allegations.

people.name: David Ferrie
people.description: Oglesby describes a figure linked in the text to guerrilla camps and Shaw.

people.name: Frank Sturgis
people.description: Oglesby describes a participant associated with the closed No Name Key base and later Watergate.

people.name: Jim Garrison
people.description: Oglesby describes the investigator whose inquiries and depositions from witnesses Oglesby discusses.

people.name: Rose Cherami
people.description: Oglesby describes a former Ruby nightclub worker whose alleged advance knowledge and statements about Ruby and Oswald are reported through investigators.

people.name: Francis Fruge
people.description: Oglesby describes the officer who encountered Cherami and later investigated her account and death.

people.name: Julia Ann Mercer
people.description: Oglesby describes the witness who, in her deposition to Garrison, disputed official reports of her identification of a truck driver as Ruby.

people.name: Lewis McWillie
people.description: Oglesby describes a Havana and Las Vegas gambling figure who maintained contacts with Ruby.

people.name: Joe Tonahill
people.description: Oglesby describes an attorney whose relationship with Ruby was openly hostile during commission questioning.

people.name: Bell P. Herndon
people.description: Oglesby describes the examiner conducting Ruby’s lengthy July 1964 test and later discussing limits on its interpretation.

people.name: Dorothy Kilgallen
people.description: Oglesby describes a columnist who obtained Ruby testimony and interviewed him privately, then died before developing a further claimed lead.

people.name: Robert McNamara
people.description: Oglesby describes the defense secretary associated with a withdrawal study and public announcement of plans to reduce American forces in Vietnam.

people.name: Maxwell Taylor
people.description: Oglesby describes the military leader whose mission with McNamara to Saigon preceded withdrawal announcements.

people.name: Ngo Dinh Diem
people.description: Oglesby describes the ruler overthrown and killed in November 1963; Oglesby distinguishes authorization of the coup from disputed authorization of murder.

people.name: Duong Van Minh
people.description: Oglesby describes the general described as taking over after Diem’s fall and supporting negotiations.

people.name: Clark Clifford
people.description: Oglesby describes a leading official whom Oglesby associates with the 1968 turn toward negotiations.

people.name: Averell Harriman
people.description: Oglesby describes an official involved in setting up the Paris peace talks.

people.name: Cyrus Vance
people.description: Oglesby describes an official involved in peace talks and the Pueblo crisis.

people.name: George Ball
people.description: Oglesby describes a senior official assigned to the United Nations during the 1968 policy turn.

people.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
people.description: Oglesby describes the leader murdered in April 1968, whose case Oglesby compares with disputed aspects of the Kennedy assassinations.

people.name: James Earl Ray
people.description: Oglesby describes Ray’s guilty plea and subsequent assertions of innocence, which the author treats as reasons to seek a new investigation.

people.name: Percy Foreman
people.description: Oglesby describes the lawyer representing Ray and previously Ruby, whose legal tactics and book-rights interests the author criticizes.

people.name: Coretta Scott King
people.description: Oglesby describes King’s widow supporting a new investigation, quoted as doubting that an impartial inquiry had occurred.

people.name: Sirhan Sirhan
people.description: Oglesby describes the accused gunman whose weapon and position Oglesby compares with disputed forensic evidence. The author’s alternate-shooter implication is an interpretation.

organizations.name: Yankees — Oglesby’s analytical grouping
organizations.description: Oglesby describes an informal model of established Northeastern finance and Atlantic-oriented power, with exceptions rather than a fixed roster.

organizations.name: Cowboys — Oglesby’s analytical grouping
organizations.description: Oglesby describes an informal model of Southwestern and Western entrepreneurial, military and Pacific-oriented power, not a formal organization.

organizations.name: Central Intelligence Agency
organizations.description: Oglesby describes an intelligence organization with competing internal centers, explicitly distinguishing factions from the whole agency.

organizations.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the federal investigative agency and domestic counterintelligence actor criticized in the book.

organizations.name: Warren Commission
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the presidential assassination inquiry whose findings and procedures the author disputes.

organizations.name: Dallas Police Department
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the municipal force involved in arresting Oswald, securing his custody and investigating the assassination.

organizations.name: Cuban Revolutionary Council
organizations.description: Oglesby describes an anti-Castro exile organization the author describes as CIA-created through Hunt.

organizations.name: Fair Play for Cuba Committee
organizations.description: Oglesby describes a pro-Castro organization whose New Orleans chapter was represented by Oswald in the book’s account.

organizations.name: Carousel Club
organizations.description: Oglesby describes Ruby’s Dallas nightclub and a setting for alleged witness observations.

organizations.name: Texas School Book Depository
organizations.description: Oglesby describes Oswald’s workplace and the building identified in the commission reconstruction as the origin of shots.

organizations.name: Organized-crime Syndicate — Oglesby’s grouping
organizations.description: Oglesby describes a network of criminal operations associated by the author with Lansky and Luciano, not a single formally incorporated organization.

organizations.name: Gehlen Organization
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the intelligence apparatus the author says moved from Nazi service into American and West German arrangements.

organizations.name: Office of Strategic Services
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the American wartime intelligence organization involved in the author’s account of postwar Gehlen incorporation.

organizations.name: Office of Naval Intelligence
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the naval intelligence service connected to Operation Underworld origins and a CIA report about Oswald.

organizations.name: Joint Chiefs of Staff
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the senior military body central to disputes over intervention and defense policy.

organizations.name: United States Department of Defense
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the defense apparatus at the center of the author’s account of policy struggles.

organizations.name: United States Department of State
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the foreign-policy department dealing with Cuba and Oswald’s travel and citizenship.

organizations.name: Hughes business interests
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the business network whose Watergate involvement Oglesby explores provisionally.

organizations.name: Chase Manhattan Bank
organizations.description: Oglesby describes a banking emblem for the author’s model of established Yankee financial power.

organizations.name: Council on Foreign Relations
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the international-affairs institution Oglesby reads through Quigley’s account of the Round Table and Eastern Establishment.

organizations.name: Round Table movement
organizations.description: Oglesby describes an English-speaking policy network described through Quigley, whose alleged American influence informs Oglesby’s model.

organizations.name: John Birch Society
organizations.description: Oglesby describes a right-wing movement with an elite-conspiracy interpretation that Oglesby explicitly distinguishes from his competing-factions model.

organizations.name: Assassination Information Bureau
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the research group advocating reopening the Kennedy investigation and a broader study of Oswald’s associations.

organizations.name: Students for a Democratic Society
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the student group organizing the April 1965 national march against the Vietnam War.

organizations.name: Las Vegas Sun
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the newspaper whose editor Hank Greenspun held documents targeted by a reported burglary plot.

organizations.name: CBS News
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the broadcaster whose assassination coverage and interviews Oglesby critically examines.

organizations.name: International Brotherhood of Teamsters
organizations.description: Oglesby describes the union whose pension-fund and organized-crime connections were targets of Robert Kennedy’s investigations in the author’s account.

events.title: Lansky visits Batista in Havana
events.description: Oglesby describes Lansky and Batista forming liquor-supply and gambling arrangements in Havana; the chronology is the author’s account.

events.title: Normandie fire and wartime intelligence bargain
events.description: Oglesby describes the liner fire as a catalyst for naval cooperation with organized crime; sabotage and bargain interpretations remain attributed.

events.title: Allied landing and Sicilian Mafia cooperation
events.description: Oglesby describes the landing in Sicily and an alleged use of Mafia local support; claimed effects on Mafia restoration are his interpretation.

events.title: Gehlen hides wartime intelligence archives
events.description: Oglesby describes Gehlen’s aides selecting and burying intelligence records before negotiating with the Americans.

events.title: Gehlen arrives in Washington
events.description: Oglesby describes Gehlen arriving for talks with American intelligence leaders about employing his network; specific conditions are source-reported.

events.title: Danner meets Nixon at Smathers gathering
events.description: Oglesby describes Danner first meeting Nixon at a party given by the newly elected Smathers.

events.title: Ruby moves to Dallas
events.description: Oglesby describes Ruby arriving in Dallas in the same year as a Chicago criminal group; the suggested takeover connection is an allegation attributed to witnesses.

events.title: Oswald seeks early Marine discharge
events.description: Oglesby describes Oswald obtaining an early hardship discharge and then traveling toward the Soviet Union; the covert-mission explanation is a hypothesis.

events.title: Kennedy–Johnson coalition wins presidency
events.description: Oglesby describes Kennedy defeating Nixon with Johnson as running mate; he interprets both tickets through his regional faction model.

events.title: Bay of Pigs invasion fails
events.description: Oglesby describes the invasion failing amid disputes over support, which he interprets as internal policy conflict rather than a unified presidential project.

events.title: Kennedy discusses assassination proposal with Szulc
events.description: Oglesby describes Szulc’s later account of Kennedy testing his response to assassinating Castro and then expressing opposition; this is reported recollection.

events.title: Oswald returns from Soviet Union
events.description: Oglesby describes Oswald and Marina returning with State Department assistance and later encountering anti-Communist associates.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis intensifies internal disputes
events.description: Oglesby describes the missile confrontation and the pressures on Kennedy; the military-overthrow concern appears through a cited memoir and is not established independently.

events.title: Kennedy proposes ending oil-depletion allowance
events.description: Oglesby describes the proposed change provoking oil-industry opposition; any linkage to assassination motives is Oglesby’s interpretation.

events.title: Kennedy announces end to raids on Cuba
events.description: Oglesby describes the announcement stopping American-based raids and a police report of anger among exiles.

events.title: Oswald moves to New Orleans
events.description: Oglesby describes the Oswalds moving to New Orleans and the author’s disputed account of associations with Shaw and Ferrie.

events.title: Oswald arrested during leaflet confrontation
events.description: Oglesby describes an arrest after confrontation with anti-Castro Cubans and Oswald asking to speak to the FBI.

events.title: Federal raids close anti-Castro camps
events.description: Oglesby describes Kennedy ordering FBI action against guerrilla bases in Florida and Louisiana; the author’s links to Ferrie and Sturgis remain source claims.

events.title: Oswald’s reported Mexico City visit
events.description: Oglesby describes the reported trip and embassy contacts, while questioning whether surveillance descriptions and impersonation claims identify Oswald reliably.

events.title: McNamara announces planned troop withdrawal
events.description: Oglesby describes a plan to withdraw 1,000 Americans before year end; his conclusion about Kennedy’s intended long-term disengagement is an interpretation.

events.title: Diem government overthrown
events.description: Oglesby describes the November 1–2 overthrow and murders of Diem and Nhu, distinguishing coup authorization from uncertainty over authorization of murder.

events.title: Cherami encountered on Louisiana roadside
events.description: Oglesby describes Cherami found injured by Fruge and subsequently making reported statements about Ruby and the assassination; these are witness allegations.

events.title: Kennedy assassinated at Dealey Plaza
events.description: Oglesby describes Kennedy killed and Connally wounded in Dallas; the author disputes the commission reconstruction and advances a coup hypothesis.

events.title: Ruby kills Oswald in police custody
events.description: Oglesby describes Ruby shooting Oswald during a jail transfer; alleged conspiracy motives are the author’s interpretation.

events.title: Commission privately discusses Oswald and FBI
events.description: Oglesby describes a secret commission session later disclosed through litigation, including doubts about investigation handling.

events.title: Commission discusses alleged Oswald informer ties
events.description: Oglesby describes commissioners considering an allegation of FBI payments and discussing difficulties proving secret relationships.

events.title: Connally disputes shared-bullet account
events.description: Oglesby describes Connally testifying that he believed his wound came from a different shot than Kennedy’s first wound.

events.title: Ruby testifies to Warren and Ford
events.description: Oglesby describes Ruby requesting transfer to Washington and a lie-detector test; Oglesby reads the ambiguous testimony as suggesting fears of a larger plot.

events.title: Hoover reports neutron-activation comparisons
events.description: Oglesby describes Hoover’s letter about lead-fragment comparisons; the author’s categorical interpretation is a scientific claim requiring separate verification.

events.title: Ruby undergoes lengthy FBI polygraph
events.description: Oglesby describes Ruby’s test and subsequent discussion of fatigue, observers and interpretive limits.

events.title: SDS organizes national antiwar march
events.description: Oglesby describes twenty to twenty-five thousand people hearing student and civil-rights speakers at a Washington protest.

events.title: Cherami dies in Texas road incident
events.description: Oglesby describes the death ruled accidental after a road collision; the author reports investigative doubts without establishing murder.

events.title: Kilgallen dies before developing assassination lead
events.description: Oglesby describes her death ruled accidental after she told associates about a potential lead; the disappearance of notes is reported as unresolved.

events.title: Ruby dies in custody
events.description: Oglesby describes Ruby’s death after illness, alongside his allegation that he was being poisoned; the allegation is not established.

events.title: Gold-outflow crisis affects Vietnam policy debate
events.description: Oglesby describes the January–February crisis as exposing economic vulnerability and sharpening elite policy disputes.

events.title: Johnson withdraws from presidential race
events.description: Oglesby describes Johnson’s decision not to run and move toward negotiations, interpreted by the author as elite pressure rather than independently proven conspiracy.

events.title: King assassinated
events.description: Oglesby describes King’s killing and disputed witness, ballistics and defense accounts, arguing for renewed investigation.

events.title: Hoover issues New Left counterintelligence memos
events.description: Oglesby describes memos directing efforts to expose and disrupt New Left organizations.

events.title: Robert Kennedy assassination disrupts election coalition
events.description: Oglesby describes the assassination and contested forensic claims; he interprets its political effect as ending a possible change in Vietnam policy.

events.title: Nixon discusses Bay of Pigs during Watergate cover-up
events.description: Oglesby describes taped Oval Office discussions with Haldeman about Hunt and CIA connections; the broader hidden connection is a hypothesis.

relationships.label: intellectual influence
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the historian’s account of elite networks informed the book’s faction model.

relationships.label: author’s faction classification
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Kennedy is classified as a left-wing Yankee in the author’s analytical model.

relationships.label: author’s faction classification
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Nixon is classified as a right-wing Cowboy.

relationships.label: author’s economic archetype
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Hughes embodies entrepreneurial Cowboy wealth in the model.

relationships.label: author’s faction classification
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Johnson is treated as a Cowboy-aligned president.

relationships.label: author’s faction classification
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Connally is placed within the Texas-oriented political grouping.

relationships.label: electoral coalition and policy conflict
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the 1960 electoral partnership later faced disputes over Cuba, Vietnam and political control.

relationships.label: political feud
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two were rivals within the Democratic governing coalition.

relationships.label: Texas visit advocacy
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Connally pressed Kennedy to visit Texas to repair party divisions.

relationships.label: White House discussions
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two discussed Hunt, the CIA and Bay of Pigs during recorded cover-up conversations.

relationships.label: concern about concealed knowledge
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Nixon’s statements indicate concern over what Hunt could expose, while its ultimate meaning remains speculative.

relationships.label: reported agency consultation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Haldeman reported Gray contacting Helms about covert CIA connections.

relationships.label: intelligence service
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Hunt was connected to Cuban exile operations and agency work.

relationships.label: organization role
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Hunt created the council as a CIA-backed grouping in the author’s account.

relationships.label: business employment
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Maheu served as a top Hughes aide.

relationships.label: CIA assassination intermediary
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Maheu contacted Roselli for an operation against Castro.

relationships.label: assassination schemes
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, agency-linked activists sought to kill Castro; authorization and timing are disputed in the text.

relationships.label: criminal network association
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Roselli is situated in the criminal network later linked to CIA anti-Castro activities.

relationships.label: organized-crime partnership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Lansky and Luciano led interrelated criminal operations; the author discusses competing assessments of their roles.

relationships.label: Cuban commercial and political partnership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two cooperated over liquor supplies, gambling and political messages.

relationships.label: wartime cooperation claimed
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the author interprets Operation Underworld as a political bargain extending beyond immediate dock security.

relationships.label: wartime intelligence cooperation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, naval intelligence cooperated with the imprisoned criminal leader.

relationships.label: personal association
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Rebozo was a close Nixon associate; an early 1942 origin is proposed but not established.

relationships.label: business partnership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Smathers and Rebozo partnered in land and financial ventures.

relationships.label: social and financial intermediary
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Danner met Nixon in 1947 and later delivered Hughes funds.

relationships.label: former service
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Danner had previously worked for the Bureau.

relationships.label: wartime intelligence connection
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the author connects Gehlen’s Soviet sources to Vlassov’s anti-Bolshevik network.

relationships.label: postwar intelligence negotiation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Gehlen negotiated American sponsorship of his apparatus; institutional details require corroboration.

relationships.label: leadership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Donovan led the wartime organization and participated in Gehlen discussions.

relationships.label: postwar incorporation claimed
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the book claims the Gehlen apparatus became a core source on Russia and Eastern Europe.

relationships.label: marriage
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two married in the Soviet Union and returned together.

relationships.label: possible covert role
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the author hypothesizes a loyal CIA agent sent to penetrate renegade anti-Castro networks; he acknowledges uncertainty.

relationships.label: informant allegation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, commissioners examined allegations of informer ties, officially denied by agency representatives.

relationships.label: personal association
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, de Mohrenschildt befriended the Oswalds; claimed intelligence implications are source-attributed.

relationships.label: association alleged
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the author cites Marchetti and witness testimony for a disputed connection.

relationships.label: association alleged
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Shaw and Ferrie are linked through the author’s discussion of Garrison’s investigation.

relationships.label: anti-Castro camp links alleged
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Ferrie is associated with agency-linked guerrilla training activities.

relationships.label: anti-Castro network association
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Sturgis is placed among the invasion and staging-base participants.

relationships.label: New Orleans activism
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Oswald circulated pro-Castro literature and operated the chapter described in the book.

relationships.label: killing
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Ruby shot Oswald during the transfer from Dallas custody.

relationships.label: personal contacts and alleged liaison
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Ruby knew many officers; an organized-crime payoff role is a research allegation cited by Oglesby.

relationships.label: Cuban and casino contacts
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Ruby traveled with McWillie, received calls and sent a pistol in 1959.

relationships.label: criminal associations
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the book lists criminal contacts while contrasting the commission’s conclusion that a significant link was not established.

relationships.label: employment
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Cherami worked as a stripper at Ruby’s club, reportedly verified by investigators.

relationships.label: claimed knowledge
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Cherami’s alleged statements linked Ruby and Oswald; reported through investigators, not independently verified.

relationships.label: investigation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Fruge handled Cherami’s roadside encounter and later inquiries.

relationships.label: witness identification allegation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Mercer asserted to Garrison that Ruby drove a truck she saw before the assassination and disputed official reports.

relationships.label: deposition
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Garrison obtained Mercer’s 1968 account of the disputed identification.

relationships.label: chairmanship
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Warren chaired the presidential inquiry.

relationships.label: membership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Ford took part in deliberations and Ruby’s testimony.

relationships.label: membership
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Dulles discussed the limits of proving intelligence relationships.

relationships.label: counsel and single-bullet theory
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Specter advanced the shared-bullet reconstruction and helped question Ruby.

relationships.label: chief counsel
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Rankin managed investigative questions and confidential sessions.

relationships.label: agency reports
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Hoover sent reports concerning lead comparisons and possible Ruby informant activity.

relationships.label: records litigation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Weisberg obtained previously concealed investigative records.

relationships.label: voice-stress interpretation
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, O’Toole argued recordings showed truthful denials, a claim dependent on disputed methodology.

relationships.label: defense counsel
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Tonahill represented Ruby but Ruby objected to his presence at questioning.

relationships.label: polygraph examination
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Herndon conducted and interpreted the long July 1964 test with acknowledged limitations.

relationships.label: journalism and interview
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Kilgallen obtained testimony and interviewed Ruby privately.

relationships.label: investigative conflict
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Kennedy’s campaign against criminal links included the Teamsters and pension funds.

relationships.label: Vietnam policy mission
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two went to Saigon before reporting on the prospects for withdrawal.

relationships.label: coup-policy dispute
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the author says Kennedy authorized the coup but acknowledges uncertainty about authorization of murder.

relationships.label: author’s faction classification
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, Clifford is treated as a central figure in the faction supporting negotiations in 1968.

relationships.label: Paris negotiations
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the two helped establish peace talks.

relationships.label: domestic counterintelligence targeting
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the New Left-targeting directive applied to the political milieu in which SDS operated.

relationships.label: criticism and reopening campaign
relationships.description: According to Oglesby, the bureau advocated renewed investigation and rejected beginning with an assumption of Oswald guilt.

relationships.label: defense representation
